provenance.author: glowny-en-f
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is watering ledger arithmetic for the same site with closed task questions, base is a diagnosis of a rota that collapses in drought. Grounded external referent: the shared water tank by the gate, introduced in turn 0 and central to the whole diagnosis (it drinks from the shed roof, its depth bands drive the rationing, and it is mentioned directly before every insertion).

a: Here is the watering ledger for the site, and the figures need totalling plot by plot.
Twelve plots each draw cans from the tank, and every can holds ten litres of water.
The four corner plots take six cans a day and the eight middle plots take four.
Work out the cans drawn in one day, then turn that figure into litres.
How many litres leave the tank across one full day at those rates?
base: Our allotment rota falls apart every August, just when the beds need water the most.
Twelve plot holders share the site, and every can is filled from the tank by the gate.
The tank drinks from the shed roof and gives it back slowly through a single brass tap.
By the second dry week the early risers have drained it before the evening people arrive.
How would you share a slow tank fairly across twelve plots in a drought?

a: The four corner plots draw twenty-four cans a day at six cans for each plot.
The eight middle plots draw thirty-two cans a day at four cans for each plot.
Together the site draws fifty-six cans, which at ten litres a can is five hundred sixty litres.
Across a seven day week that daily figure grows to three thousand nine hundred twenty litres.
Does the ledger show the same fifty-six cans when the plot lines are added by hand?
base: Fairness starts with knowing what the tank actually yields in a dry week, not what people hope.
A roof fed tank in drought is living off its stored depth, and depth runs out quietly.
I would mark the inside wall of the tank with a simple painted scale before anything else.
Once you can read the level, the rota can ration by depth instead of by luck.
Do you know how many cans the tank gives up before the tap starts to gasp?

a: Now check the ledger against the tank's refill line for the same seven day week.
The roof feeds the tank three hundred litres a day when any rain falls at all.
In the week under review, rain fell on just two days out of the seven.
Set the week's refill against the week's draw and state the shortfall in litres.
How many litres short does the tank run across that whole dry week?
base: Nobody has ever measured it, and the tank keeps its own counsel behind that green lid.
We only learn the level the hard way, when the tap coughs at half past seven.
Painting a scale sounds easy enough, and my neighbour has a tin of white left over.
But a scale only tells us what is gone, not who took it or when.
Would a depth reading alone really change how people fill their cans at six in the morning?

a: Two rain days give the tank six hundred litres of refill across the week.
The draw for the week stands at three thousand nine hundred twenty litres as worked out.
Setting refill against draw leaves a shortfall of three thousand three hundred twenty litres.
In cans of ten litres, the week runs three hundred thirty-two cans short.
Is the shortfall figure to be carried forward into next week's ledger sheet?
base: A reading changes behaviour when it comes with a shared rule, never on its own.
Tie the scale to can limits: above the top mark, six cans, below it, four.
When the tank shows its lowest band, the tap closes for all but seedlings.
The early risers are not villains, they are simply first at an unmetered well.
Could your committee agree three bands and paint them before the next dry spell?

a: One correction to the ledger: plot nine is a corner plot, not a middle one.
That makes five corner plots at six cans and seven middle plots at four cans.
Recalculate the daily cans and litres, and carry the change through the weekly draw.
Then restate the weekly shortfall against the same six hundred litres of refill.
How many cans a day does the site draw after the plot nine change?
base: Three bands the committee could manage, though the word committee flatters four people and a kettle.
The tank will need a dry morning for the paint, so the job must wait for Saturday.
My worry is the lowest band, because seedlings are a word people stretch in a drought.
Half the site will swear their squash are seedlings by the middle of August.
Should the lowest band close the tap outright instead of leaving a seedling excuse?

a: Five corner plots at six cans apiece draw thirty cans between them each day.
Seven middle plots at four cans add twenty-eight cans, giving fifty-eight cans a day.
Fifty-eight cans of ten litres come to five hundred eighty litres each day.
The weekly draw is four thousand sixty litres, and the shortfall becomes three thousand four hundred sixty.
Shall the ledger carry fifty-eight cans as the new daily figure from Monday?
base: Close the tap outright at the lowest band, and put the seedling cases through a person.
One named keyholder a week can unlock the tap for genuine trays and nothing else.
People argue with a painted line, but they rarely argue with a neighbour holding a key.
Rotate the key with the rota, and let the tank's band decide when the key matters.
Would a week of key duty per plot holder be a burden anyone resents?

a: Now build the duty list for the twelve plots across a twelve week summer.
Plot one takes week one, and the plots follow in number order after that.
Weeks five and nine are swap weeks, where the named plot trades with the next number.
Write out the first ten weeks of the list with the swaps applied.
Which plot holds the key in week nine once its swap is applied?
base: Key duty would sit well beside the mowing rota, which people already accept without much grumbling.
I can pair each week's keyholder with the plot that already mows that week.
The tank, the key and the mower would then change hands together every Sunday evening.
That gives twelve turns of duty, one for each plot across the season.
What happens, though, in the week a keyholder goes away on holiday?

a: Weeks one to four go to plots one, two, three and four in plain order.
Week five is a swap week, so plot six takes it and plot five takes week six.
Weeks seven and eight go to plots seven and eight in the plain order again.
Week nine swaps too, so plot ten takes it and plot nine takes week ten.
Plot ten therefore holds the key in week nine under the swap rule.
base: Holidays are why the key should live in the shed lockbox, not in anyone's kitchen drawer.
The duty passes with the code, and a keyholder who travels simply phones the next name.
Put the season's twelve names on one laminated card inside the shed window.
Anyone standing at the tap can then see whose week it is without knocking on doors.
A rota people can read at the point of use is the one they follow.

a: Last task for tonight: total the duty weeks each plot carries across the twelve week summer.
Every plot should carry exactly one week once the two swaps are counted through.
List any plot that carries no week and any plot that carries two of them.
Then state the weeks eleven and twelve holders to close the list out.
Close with the full count of duty weeks so the sheet can be filed.
base: A lockbox we have, left over from the year the strimmer kept walking off.
I will paint the bands on Saturday, fit the card, and set the code on Sunday.
The first dry spell will tell us whether the bands hold or the arguments simply move.
Either way we will finally be arguing about a number instead of a rumour.
I will bring the whole scheme to the site meeting on the first of the month.

a: With the two swaps counted, every plot from one to ten carries exactly one duty week.
No plot carries none in that span, and no plot carries two either.
Week eleven goes to plot eleven and week twelve goes to plot twelve as listed.
That closes the list with twelve duty weeks spread across the twelve plots.
The full count stands at twelve weeks covered, and the sheet is ready to file.
base: Bring the scheme as one page: three bands, can limits, the key rule and the card.
Lead with the painted scale, because everyone has stood at that tap wondering what was left.
Save the closed tap band for last and pair it with the keyholder in the same breath.
A rule that arrives with its own mercy is far harder to vote down.
If August still beats you, at least the ledger will show exactly how.
